text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over several years, and many people have subtle or no early symptoms.

list.snippet: Frequent urination (polyuria): Needing to pee more often—especially at night—happens as your kidneys try to flush out extra blood sugar.
Increased thirst (polydipsia): Dehydration from frequent urination triggers an intense, constant need to drink.
Persistent fatigue: When your cells cannot properly absorb glucose for energy, you feel unusually tired even with adequate rest.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar causes fluid shifts that can swell the lenses of your eyes.
Increased hunger (polyphagia): Your body fails to use blood sugar for fuel properly, leaving you feeling hungry shortly after eating.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: High blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens the immune response, making minor wounds take much longer to heal.
Frequent infections: Recurring urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections happen because excess sugar in fluids and tissues encourages bacteria and fungus to grow.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety skin folds around the neck, armpits, or groin as a sign of insulin resistance.
Tingling or numbness: Early peripheral nerve damage can cause a mild prickling or loss of sensation in the hands or feet.

text_blocks.snippet: Doctors confirm Type 2 diabetes using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic or your primary care provider:

list.snippet: Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Measures your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months; 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar at any time; 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes (often paired with symptoms).
